hints.junior: Every 10-second poll re-downloads the full body, even though the underlying numbers only actually change every few minutes.
hints.mid: A TTL cache trades one problem for another — too long and a real update sits stale, too short and you're back to over-fetching.
hints.staff: What's missing is a validation step that's cheap on every request but only pays the transfer cost when there's actually new data.

hints.junior: Click Poll several times in each mode and watch the transfer total — the simulated data actually changes every fourth poll.
hints.mid: Broken always sends a plain GET and gets a full body back. Fixed sends If-None-Match after the first request and gets a 304 with 0 bytes when the ETag still matches.
hints.staff: The simulated ETag only increments when the data version actually changes, mirroring a server that hashes the current representation rather than reissuing on every request regardless of content.

hints.junior: First request: 200 OK, full body, plus an ETag. Next request sends that ETag back as If-None-Match — unchanged means a 304 with no body at all.
hints.mid: A 304 is deliberately body-less — the client's job is to keep serving its cached copy, not to treat the response as new data to render.
hints.staff: An ETag is correct by construction, not by tuning — the client never serves data staler than its last request, and never re-transfers a body the server can prove is identical.

hints.junior: A plain "abc123" ETag is a strong validator; a W/"abc123" with the W/ prefix is weak — semantically equivalent but not byte-identical.
hints.mid: Last-Modified / If-Modified-Since is the lower-resolution sibling — second-level timestamp precision instead of a content hash, cheaper when hashing the body isn't worth it.
hints.staff: A naive fetch wrapper that always calls .json() throws on a real 304 — branch on response.status === 304 before parsing, and fall back to the cached payload.

sections.junior: Today's case is about a dashboard that polls an API every ten seconds, downloading the full response every single time, even though the underlying data only actually changes every few minutes.
sections.mid: A blind cache trades one problem for another — pick the duration too long and a real update sits stale, too short and you're back to over-fetching.
sections.staff: What's missing is a cheap validation step on every request that only pays the transfer cost when there's actually new data to send.

sections.junior: The first request gets back the full body plus an e tag, a short identifier for that version of the data. The next request sends that e tag back, and if nothing changed, the server replies 304 not modified, with no body at all.
sections.mid: A 304 response is deliberately empty. The client's job is to keep using its cached copy, not to treat the response as new data.
sections.staff: The real gain over a time-based cache is that this is correct by construction. The client never serves data staler than its last request, and never re-transfers a body the server can prove hasn't changed.

sections.junior: Try clicking poll a few times in each mode and watch what happens to the running transfer total.
sections.mid: Broken always downloads the full body. Fixed only downloads it when the simulated data actually changed.
sections.staff: Notice the e tag only increments when the underlying data version changes, not on every single poll.

sections.junior: Send back the e tag you were given on the next request. If nothing changed, you get an empty reply back instead of the whole payload again.
sections.mid: This validates freshness without guessing a cache duration, and most polls become nearly free once the client already has the current version.
sections.staff: Handle the empty response explicitly in your fetch layer before trying to parse a body, and remember that no-cache means revalidate before use, not don't cache.
